The difference is which modules seat in the power tray; the chassis is the same metal either way, which is why this is a configuration and not a separate device.","kind":"orderable","part-numbers":{"ASR-9006-DC-V2":{"part":"ASR-9006-DC-V2","power-cord":"none"}}}},"description":"Cisco ASR 9006 Router - the 10RU, six-slot member of the ASR 9000 Series Aggregation Services Routers. Cards mount HORIZONTALLY: slots 0 and 1 at the bottom of the cage are reserved for a redundant RSP pair, slots 2 to 5 above them take line cards. Two fan trays sit above the cage behind a hinged door, and a single power shelf below it carries the AC or DC power modules, whose inlets are on the rear face. Modelled as a BARE CAGE: every slot is a bay that a card component drops into, not a traced faceplate.","format":1,"gaps":[{"note":"Cisco publishes no chassis-level power draw for any ASR 9000. Table 14's \"Power Dissipation\" row says only \"Use the Cisco Power Calculator ... to estimate the maximum power distribution\", so the chassis total is whatever its occupants sum to. Recorded in provenance as no-chassis-power-figure since the family was modelled; scoped here so a comparison can tell this apart from a figure nobody has looked for","reason":"vendor-silent","scope":["fact:peak-power-w","fact:typical-power-w"],"wanted":"a chassis-level maximum and typical draw from Cisco, or confirmation that the Power Calculator is the only answer the vendor will give","what":"chassis-power-figure"},{"note":"cisco/a9k-pwr-3kw-ac@1 states 142.78 mm wide. Three of them need 428.34 mm and this chassis's power shelf interior measures 416.50, so they do not fit - lint L13 flagged the overlap directly when they were placed at the measured centres. Against that, the stencil's shape box for the 'A9K Power Module' master reads 0.5477 in, which is 139.12 mm at the stencil's 1:10 scale, and my own measurement of the three openings in the ASR 9006 front master gives 138.35, 137.50 and 138.23. Those two agree to under a millimetre, and three at 139.12 come to 417.36 against a 416.50 shelf - the arithmetic a shelf that holds exactly three ought to produce. The 142.78 is most likely the art measured over something that is not the module's seating width, the same class of error as reading a card's shape box instead of its art. The bays here are sized to the measured openings, so the chassis is right and the component and the chassis disagree by about 3.7 mm until someone re-measures the master.","reason":"sources-disagree","scope":["power-modules"],"wanted":"a re-measurement of the 'A9K Power Module' stencil master, or a Cisco dimension for the version 1 power module","what":"power-module-width-disagrees-with-the-component"},{"blocks":[],"note":"NINE CARDS SHARE THESE SIX SLOTS AND TWO FAMILIES DISAGREE BY 32.8 mm ON THE ONE AXIS THAT HAS TO FIT ONE OPENING. The line cards and the blank filler are 395.7 mm; all four RSP-880 variants are 428.5. The measured cage opening is 352.59. The line-card story is coherent: a9k-slot-cover's own art measures a PLATE of 362.24 inside a 395.7 envelope, so the plate covers the 352.59 opening with 4.8 mm of overlap per side and the ejector brackets account for the remaining 16.7 per side. Every number has a job. The RSP-880's does not. 428.5 needs 37.96 mm of overlap per side to cover the same opening, and a card centred on this cage reaches x 22.99 to 451.49 in a 444.5 mm chassis - 6.99 mm PAST the outer wall, which is visible in the 3D view as the card's end standing proud of the side of the box. WHERE 428.5 COMES FROM, AND WHY IT IS THE SUSPECT: the RSP-880 data sheet's 'Physical specifications' row. This library's own a9k-rsp880-se provenance already records that NINE RSP AND RP MASTERS IN THE STENCIL ARE ONE DRAWING, scaled to four different stated widths - 402.8, 428.5, 428.2 and 403.4 - so \"the drawing is generic across the family and cannot be all four sizes\". The cage, by contrast, is measured off this chassis's own master and independently supported by Figure 19. NOT RESOLVED HERE. Two numbers describing different things is the likeliest reading - the same trap as a plate against an envelope - but nothing we hold says WHICH thing 428.5 measures, and inventing a smaller one would be the reconciliation this project keeps digging back out.","reason":"sources-disagree","scope":["slots"],"wanted":"a Cisco mechanical drawing of an RSP-880 faceplate, or one measurement across a real card from ejector tip to ejector tip. Either settles it for all four variants at once and for every chassis they go in. REQUESTED FROM THE LAB, 2026-08-26, and tracked as roc-ops/Portrayal#16 - that issue carries the three conflicting Cisco figures and what to do when the number arrives.","what":"rsp880-width-cannot-fit-this-cage"},{"note":"NARROWED, not closed. This file and the ASR 9010's carried pitches that disagreed - 46.60 here against 44.33 there - for two chassis that take the same cards. Cisco's RSP-880 sheet resolved the 9010 half: the card is 46.0 mm thick and Cisco names the 9010 among the chassis it serves, so a 44.33 slot is impossible there and that cage is now divided on published card thicknesses. THIS CHASSIS IS NOT DISCRIMINATED BY THAT EVIDENCE. Its 279.63 mm cage admits both readings: four line card slots at 41.4 plus two RSP slots at 46.0 is 257.6, leaving 22.03 for guides; and an even six-way division at 46.60 is also >= 46.0 and so also admits the RSP-880. The even division is kept because it is what the cage measures and because nothing here favours the other, but it is an assumption and the 9010 shows the family does not always divide evenly. Neither this master nor the 9010's prints slot labels or draws cage dividers, which is why both were assumptions in the first place - the 9904, 9906, 9910, 9912 and 9922 all have a ruler in the picture and these two do not.","reason":"needs-drawing","scope":["slots"],"wanted":"a dimensioned front elevation of the ASR 9006, or a per-slot width from any Cisco document","what":"slot-pitch-even-division-is-unconfirmed"},{"note":"Two figures in b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide.pdf give the ASR 9006 body width differently. Table 13 \"Cisco ASR 9000 Series Routers Physical Descriptions\" (p130) says 17.50 inches (44.45 cm). Figure 9 \"Cisco ASR 9006 Router Chassis Footprint Dimensions - Top Down View\" (p24) dimensions the same body at 17.38 inches (44.15 cm). Same measure, same part, 3 mm apart, so this is a real conflict and not two scopes. The manifest carries 44.45 because the spec table is authoritative for overall dimensions and because Cisco's own Visio master independently records 1.9 in at 1:10 over the flanges, which back-solves to Table 13's split once the 19.05 mm flange protrusion is subtracted. The likeliest reconciliation is that 17.50 is over the outer skin and 17.38 is the sheet metal at the section plane Figure 9 cuts, but no document we hold says that, so it is not written as though one does. The height is unaffected - both sources and the stencil agree on 17.50 in there.","reason":"sources-disagree","scope":["front","rear","top","bottom"],"wanted":"a Cisco mechanical drawing with a tolerance, or a tape measure on a real ASR 9006","what":"chassis-width-sources-disagree"},{"note":"The power modules load from the front but their inlets are on the rear, and the only artwork we hold for that rear panel is the stencil's ASR-9006-AC Rear master, which draws the VERSION 1 tray: three IEC inlets labelled M2, M1, M0 left to right (mirrored from the front's M0, M1, M2) with the legend \"100-240V 50/60 Hz 16A MAX (3X)\" and a yellow warning label. This chassis is modelled as version 2, which has four modules and therefore four inlets, and no figure in any document we hold shows the version 2 rear panel. Rather than mirror three inlets into four and invent a pitch, the rear carries the inlet panel's outer band only. The DC rear is a further unknown again - there is no ASR-9006-DC master in the stencil at all.","reason":"needs-drawing","scope":["rear"],"wanted":"a figure or photograph of the version 2 AC rear panel, and of the DC rear panel","what":"rear-power-inlet-detail"},{"note":"The air filter is real, sourced and correctly typed as a bay - Table 17 of b-asr9k-hardware-installation-guide.pdf places it along the right side accessible from the rear, and Figure 207 shows the panel and its thumb screw. What is NOT sourced is its geometry. Figure 207 is a three-quarter perspective view with no dimension lines on it, so its aspect is foreshortened and it fails gate 1 as a source of absolute size. The filter's 52 mm width and its 8 mm standoff from the rear edge are read as fractions of that figure and anchored to the chassis depth, and its height is set to the card cage band rather than measured. Treat the filter's extent as the one feature here that a tape measure would most likely move. Its presence, its side, its access direction and the fact that it is user-replaceable are all stated in words by the guide and are not in doubt.","reason":"needs-drawing","scope":["right","filters"],"wanted":"a dimensioned side elevation of the ASR 9006, or the air filter's own spare-part drawing","what":"air-filter-position"},{"note":"Seven measured openings on this chassis have no occupant in the library: fan trays FT0 and FT1 (175.65 x 70.97 each), power modules M0 to M3 (103.22 x 46.34 each) and the right-side air filter (52 x 279.63). All seven are drawn as cutouts, so the sheet metal is complete and every dimension is recorded; what is absent is the parts. This is NOT the machine-findable kind of gap - a missing ref lints - but the fact that these openings are cutouts rather than bays IS invisible to any rule, and a reader could reasonably assume the chassis simply has no fan bays. It has them; they are waiting. Cisco's own numbering for them is FT0/FT1 and M0-M3 per Figure 19, and the groups are ready to be reinstated with index-origin 0.","reason":"needs-drawing","scope":["front","right"],"wanted":"an ASR 9006 fan tray, the version 2 AC and DC power modules, and the chassis air filter","what":"openings-awaiting-components"},{"note":"RENAMED FROM blank-faces AND REWORDED, because both faces stopped being blank and the gap was still describing the file as it stood two commits ago. NO DOCUMENT WE HOLD SHOWS EITHER FACE OF AN ASR 9006 - that part is unchanged and is the gap. What each face now carries is derived from a figure of a DIFFERENT face, which is a weaker thing than being drawn and is why the gap stays open. The bottom carries the rack mounting surface, because the plane is dimensioned in Figure 9's top-down view and necessarily cuts the underside at the same depth it cuts the top. The left carries one of the three NEBS bonding points, because Figure 58 callouts a left-side pad and its position is INFERRED from a three-quarter view rather than dimensioned. Neither is a bottom or left drawing; both are a fact about the chassis that has to intersect this face. Everything else about these two faces - feet, labels, vents, plates, the flange profile - is still unknown, and the guide's \"There is no clearance requirement for the left side of the chassis\" (b-asr9k-hardware-installation-guide.pdf p1172) is consistent with a solid unfeatured panel without proving one. The sizes are from Table 13 and Figure 9 and are right, so the rack elevation and the 3D box are right, which is the load these two views actually carry.","reason":"vendor-silent","scope":["bottom","left"],"wanted":"a six-face photograph set, or the mechanical drawings behind Figure 9","what":"undocumented-faces"}],"groups":{"doors":{"index-origin":0,"physical-context":"Chassis","role":"furniture","term":"Door"},"grounding":{"index-origin":1,"role":"furniture","term":"Point"},"power-modules":{"attrs":{"redundancy":"n+1","redundancy-note":"n+1 - the AC and DC power trays in the ASR 9006 and ASR 9904 both provide N+1 redundancy (Overview and Reference Guide, Power System). The install guide adds that at least two AC power modules are required for N+1 on a fully configured system"},"index-origin":0,"physical-context":"PowerSupply","role":"service","term":"Power Module"},"slots":{"index-origin":0,"physical-context":"NetworkingDevice","role":"traffic","term":"Slot"}},"kind":"device","manufacturer":"Cisco","maturity":"modelled","model":"ASR 9006","name":"asr-9006","portfolio":{"family":"Aggregation Services Router","line":"Service Provider","series":"ASR 9000 Series"},"provenance":{"air-filter":"datasheet - Table 17 \"Air Filter Locations for the Cisco ASR 9000 Series Routers\", b-asr9k-hardware-installation-guide.pdf p228: \"Cisco ASR 9006 Router - Located along the right side of the chassis and is accessible from the rear.\" Figure 207 \"Replacing the Cisco ASR 9006 Router Chassis Air Filter\" (p230) draws it: a tall narrow panel with a thumb screw, withdrawn rearwards from the right side. It slides into an opening, so per rule 6 it is a BAY and not a placement, and the empty bay showing an opening is what a 9006 with its filter out looks like. Its position on the right face is read from Figure 207 as fractions - rear end of the side, spanning the card cage height band - and anchored to the depth and cage extents known from elsewhere. That is the least certain geometry in this manifest and is flagged in gaps","airflow":"datasheet - \"Cisco ASR 9006 Router: Side-to-top to rear cooling path. The inlet is at the right side of the chassis, and the exhaust is at the upper rear\", b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide.pdf p3725, repeated at p2827. Hence chassis.airflow side, a right-side intake grille on the right view and the exhaust grille on the rear","bay-size-is-the-reserved-space-opening-is-the-hole":"ONE FIELD WAS DOING TWO JOBS. `size` is what the slot RESERVES - where the card is placed and what it is checked against - and on this cage that is the card including its ejector brackets, 395.7 x 41.4. The renderer also painted that rectangle dark, so 21.56 mm of \"opening\" was drawn over sheet metal at each end, and the owner could see black past the edges of an installed card. `opening` now names the second job: 352.59 x 46.605, the cage measured off the front master at 60.94 to 413.53 across and six bands of 46.605 from 104.63 down. The bays are unchanged from the arbitration that a bay and its occupant carry the same size, so nothing about placement or checking moves. CHECKED AGAINST FIGURE 19 BEFORE TRUSTING IT, at the owner's suggestion. That figure's front face has vertical left and right edges, so horizontal fractions off it are valid: the opening reads about 358 wide with a 63.5 mm left inset against 352.59 and 60.94 here. The cage was never the problem. THE ASYMMETRY IS REAL. 60.94 mm of metal left and 30.97 right, because the master draws a wide vertical strip on the left carrying the ESD receptacle and only a card rail on the right. Figure 19 shows the same, and the power shelf below - which has no such strip - is symmetric.","bottom-face":"DECLARED EMPTY BY VERIFICATION, not by omission, and this is the wording the team lead asked for. THERE IS NO BOTTOM VIEW OF ANY ASR 9000 CHASSIS IN THE ENTIRE 78-DOCUMENT CORPUS: asr9k-chassis searched every figure caption in all 65 PDFs for \"Bottom View\", \"underside\" and \"bottom of the chassis\" and got zero hits. That is an exhaustive search returning nothing, not a failure to look. So no feet, no labels, no vents and no plate are drawn here, because nothing is known about this face. WHAT IS DRAWN is the rack mounting surface, and it is here on geometric necessity rather than because a bottom figure shows it: the mounting plane is dimensioned in the top-down figure and it necessarily cuts this face at the same depth it cuts the top, in the same way an integral rack flange shows on every face it meets. THE ABSENCE IS NOT ANNOTATED AS CONTENT - there is no region here saying the underside is undocumented, because passing a content check by describing a hole is the thing this project has spent the session removing. If the capability change under discussion lands, this face should be read as deliberately empty","cage-asymmetry":"drawing - the cage is NOT centred in the body: 60.94 mm of metal to its left and 30.97 mm to its right. That is real, not a measurement error - the front master draws a wide vertical strip on the left carrying the ESD receptacle, and only a card rail on the right. The power shelf below it, which has no such strip, is symmetric","cage-opening-not-drawn-separately":"the card cage is NOT declared as its own cutout. It was, and it hid the thing it was meant to show: a full-width black opening behind the bays swallowed the guides between them, so ten slots rendered as one black mass. The bays already describe the openings and the cage's measured extent is recorded above, so the separate cutout was redundant as well as harmful. The other five chassis in this family never had one, and this brings these two into line","calibration-check":"measured - the calibration was checked before it was used, not after. Taking the front master's ink bounding box as 482.6 mm wide (flange tip to flange tip) and 444.5 mm tall gives 0.12083 and 0.12195 mm/px at a 4000 px render. The power shelf then comes out at 13.94 mm from the body left edge and 14.06 mm from the body right edge - symmetric to 0.12 mm, which nothing forced. That is an independent confirmation of both the scale and the 19.05 mm flange protrusion","callout-audit":"the guide's own overview figure was walked callout by callout, which is the check that caught a missing grounding point on the first device built to this skill. Figure 3 \"Cisco ASR 9006 Router Chassis Components\": fan tray door (two fan trays) -> ft-0, ft-1 with the door itself deferred to a component; rear air exhaust -> the rear grille decor; side air intake -> the right view grille; four slots for line cards -> slot-2 to slot-5; two bottom slots reserved for redundant RSPs -> slot-0, slot-1; power shelf -> the shelf cutout; four AC/DC or DC/DC power modules -> pm-0 to pm-3. Rack mount bracket is the one callout DELIBERATELY not modelled, because this manifest draws the body and not the flanges. Figure 9 adds the rack mounting surface -> the top view. HIG Table 17 adds the air filter, HIG p125 and Figure 133 add the grounding receptacle, and the stencil masters add the ESD receptacle and the rear inlet panel. Every one of those is present","card-compatibility":"datasheet - and this is Cisco stating it directly rather than being inferred from geometry. The per-card datasheets carry a \"Chassis compatibility\" row, and datasheet-c78-743580, \"Cisco ASR 9000 Series 5th Generation High-Density Multi-Rate Line Cards: 2 Terabit and 0.8 Terabit Cards\", says of A9K-20HG-FLEX-SE, -TR, A9K-8HG-FLEX-SE and -TR: \"Compatible with the Cisco ASR 9006, ASR 9010, ASR 9904, ASR 9906, ASR 9910, ASR 9912, and ASR 9922 chassis\". All seven, this chassis among them, so those four are in every card slot's accepts alongside the blank. The row is per-DATASHEET and does not extend to cards it does not cover: the ASR 9900-only parts (A99-32X100GE, A99-10X400GE-X and the 16-port Service Edge) name only the 9900 chassis in their own rows and are deliberately absent here. A card is listed when a Cisco document says it fits, not when it would physically go in","card-orientation":"datasheet - stated directly, and it had been an inference until now. The Overview and Reference Guide's \"Chassis Slots\" section (b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide.pdf p17) names every chassis in the family and gives the ejector position as the tell: \"Cisco ASR 9006 Router and Cisco ASR 9904 Router: All chassis line cards and RSP cards are front-facing and mounted horizontally, with ejector levers and captive screws at the left and right ends of each card\". A bay therefore places a card component rotated. Only the ASR 9006 and ASR 9904 are horizontal; the 9010, 9906, 9910, 9912 and 9922 all stand their cards up, including the 21 RU 9010. This section supersedes the three-way inference an earlier revision rested on - the slot figures, Figure 2's \"four on each side\" callout and the measured cage aspect - all of which agreed with it.","chassis":"datasheet - Table 13 \"Cisco ASR 9000 Series Routers Physical Descriptions\", b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide.pdf p130. ASR 9006: chassis height 17.50 in (44.45 cm), chassis width 17.50 in (44.45 cm) with \"19.0 inches (48.3 cm) including chassis rack-mount flanges and front door width\", chassis depth 28.93 in (73.48 cm) \"from the rear cover to the front of the cosmetic doors\". Modelled as the BODY, 444.5 x 444.5 x 734.8 mm, so the front face of this chassis is square. The rack-mount flanges take it to 482.6 mm and are deliberately not drawn, following the C100G precedent in this library","colour":"drawing - light grey sheet metal with a near-black card cage and power shelf interior, from the front master","compliance":"datasheet - data_sheet_c78-501767.pdf, series compliance list: \"SR-3580: NEBS Criteria Levels (Level 3)\", \"GR-1089-CORE: NEBS EMC and Safety\", \"GR-63-CORE: NEBS Physical Protection\". Transcribed as printed. This is a series-level claim, not an ASR 9006-specific certificate","depth":"datasheet - 28.93 in (73.48 cm), stated identically by Table 13 and by Figure 9's own dimension line. Two sources, no disagreement. Figure 9 also puts the rack mounting surface 5.73 in (14.55 cm) back from the front of the chassis","depth-axis-on-side-views":"FOUR FEATURES ON THIS CHASSIS WERE AT THE WRONG END OF THEIR VIEW, and they were wrong because no file stated which end of a left or right view is the front. The convention is derivable and now is: kit/viewer3d.js builds each face in local coordinates (x right, y up, z out of the face) and orients it with a fixed rotation, front at +z and rear at -z. Right is rot [0, +pi/2, 0], sending local +x to world -z, so ON A RIGHT VIEW x = 0 IS THE FRONT AND x = depth IS THE REAR. Left is rot [0, -pi/2, 0], sending local +x to world +z, so ON A LEFT VIEW x = 0 IS THE REAR. The box-UV path and viewer3d.js's own component-branch comment both give the same answer. WHAT MOVED, all of it derived by subtracting from the 734.8 depth rather than re-measured: the right-side NEBS ground pad from x 26.0 to 662.8, the air filter opening from 8.0 to 674.8, the right intake grille from 64.0 to 110.8 so its clearance to the filter is preserved, and the left-side NEBS pad from 662.8 to 26.0. Every one of those is a feature this file already DOCUMENTED as being at the rear - the guide puts the ground pad at the \"upper rear corner\" and Table 17 makes the air filter \"accessible from the rear\" - so the words were right and only the coordinates were wrong. THE TWO GROUND PADS HAD EXACTLY SWAPPED PLACES, 26.0 and 662.8 each sitting where the other belonged, which is the signature of mirroring left from right by copying x when the correct mirror is depth - x - width. Nothing here needed a new source; the file disagreed with itself and the labels were the half that was right.","electrical":"datasheet - Table 15 (AC) and Table 16 (DC), pp132-135. The ASR 9006 columns only. THE CHASSIS BRANDING IS ON THAT DOOR. The stencil front master prints the cisco logo and \"Cisco ASR 9000 Series\" on the door face, so per the skill that text is the door component's own silkscreen and is deliberately absent from this chassis manifest. The door itself is a placement waiting on a component from library/components/cisco/ - see gaps","fan-trays":"datasheet + drawing - Figure 19 gives two fan trays FT0 and FT1 side by side above the card cage. The front master puts the seam between them at 237.85 mm, which is the cage midpoint (237.24) to within 0.6 mm. The band runs 0 to 104.63 mm, of which the top 33.66 mm is a shroud and the rest is the door face. The overview guide adds that \"Each fan tray has six fans arranged in three groups of two fans each\" (p2827)","grounding":"datasheet - the ASR 9006's grounding receptacle is \"Top rear right side of the chassis\", b-asr9k-hardware-installation-guide.pdf p125, Table of grounding receptacle locations. Figure 133 \"NEBS Bonding and Grounding for the Cisco ASR 9006 Router\" (p127) shows it unambiguously: a two-hole lug pad bolted to the upper rear corner of the perforated RIGHT side panel, with a detail circle showing two screws through a flat lug. Drawn as a cutout on the right view at the rear-top corner. This is the callout the skill warns about - the first device built to this skill shipped without a grounding point because nobody went looking for one, so it was looked for here on purpose","left-face":"datasheet + drawing, with the POSITION stated as inferred. This chassis has THREE NEBS bonding and grounding points, not one: the guide says to connect \"to one of the three supplemental bonding and grounding connections on the back or side of the router chassis\", and Figure 58 callouts them as right side, rear and LEFT side. So a left-side point exists and this face is not blank. Its position is INFERRED - Figure 58 is a three-quarter view from below and draws the pad low and rearward, so it is placed at the rear-lower corner, mirroring the right pad's x and flipping its y. The grounding RECEPTACLE is a different thing and is separately documented at \"Top rear right side of the chassis\", which is where the right view already carries it. ORIENTATION CORRECTED: this file said \"this view mirrors the right, so the REAR is at x = 734.8\" and that is backwards. On a LEFT view the rear is at x = 0. See depth-axis-on-side-views","left-face-has-no-vent":"stated rather than left to be wondered about. The cooling path is side-to-top-to-rear - \"the inlet is at the right side of the chassis, and the exhaust is at the upper rear\" - so unlike the right face, which is mostly perforation, the left face carries no air opening at all. Drawing a grille here to balance the right would be inventing one","lifecycle":"datasheet - searched, and the finding is a distinction rather than a date. Cisco bulletin EOL9675 (Amended), \"End-of-Sale and End-of-Life Announcement for the Cisco ASR 9000 Series Version 1 Power Bundles and Devices\", updated 23 December 2019, lists ASR-9006-AC and ASR-9006-DC as end-of-sale, replaced by ASR-9006-AC-V2 and ASR-9006-DC-V2. But its migration section says verbatim: \"The Cisco ASR 9006 and ASR 9010 chassis continue their regular support as part of the Cisco ASR 9000 Series, and these can continue to be purchased together with the Version 2 AC or DC power trays ... Only those products related to Version 1 power bundles and devices are part of this end-of-sale notice.\" So the CHASSIS has no EoL announced; the version 1 POWER BUNDLE PID does. Both facts are recorded, because recording only the first would read as \"nobody looked\" and only the second would retire a product Cisco still sells","no-cable-management-tray":"searched and ABSENT, which is a finding rather than an omission. The ASR 9010 has a cable management tray - Figure 2 calls it out and Figure 15 illustrates it - and the guide's text scopes that section to the 9010: \"The following image shows how card interface cables are managed at the front of the Cisco ASR 9010 Router chassis using a cable management tray.\" Table 13 corroborates by measuring the two chassis differently: the 9010's depth is quoted \"including the cable management system and front cover\", the 9006's only \"from the rear cover to the front of the cosmetic doors\". So the 9006 is not modelled with one, on purpose","no-chassis-power-figure":"NOTE - Cisco publishes NO chassis-level power draw for any ASR 9000. Table 14's \"Power Dissipation\" row says only \"Use the Cisco Power Calculator ... to estimate the maximum power distribution\". So there is deliberately no power-max-w or power-typical-w here: the chassis total is whatever its occupants sum to, and while the card components are unbuilt that total is zero rather than low. This is the vendor being silent, not this model being thin","openings-without-occupants":"the two fan trays, the four power modules and the air filter are drawn as CUTOUTS rather than bays, and the distinction is deliberate. A bay must name a component that fits it, and a9k-slot-cover is a LINE CARD AND RSP blank - its own description says so - so a 41.4 x 395.7 filler plate does not cover a 175.65 x 70.97 fan tray opening or a 103.22 x 46.34 power module one. Pointing them at it would have linted clean at the cost of seven false compatibility claims. Drawing them as cutouts keeps every measurement in the file and the metal correct, and states nothing about what goes in them. They become bays when the ASR 9006 fan tray and the version 2 AC and DC power modules exist in library/components/cisco/ - the geometry is already here and the change is mechanical","power-inlets-are-on-the-rear":"drawing - the power MODULES load from the front shelf, but their AC inlets are on the REAR face. Two independent sources put the module near 139 instead: the stencil's own shape box for that master reads 0.5477 in, i.e. 139.12 at 1:10, and three of those come to 417.36 against a 416.50 shelf, which is the arithmetic a shelf holding exactly three should produce. The guide states the split in words on p3: \"The version 1 power system has three power modules in the single power tray. The version 2 power system has four power modules in the single power tray\", and notes \"The ASR 9006 chassis does not support version 3 power modules\"","power-tray-generation":"the shelf is modelled as the VERSION 1 tray, three modules, because that is what the master draws and what there are measurements for. The version 2 tray holds four narrower modules - Figure 19 numbers them M0 to M3, Figure 3 is captioned \"Version 2 Power Tray Shown\" and Table 15 says four per tray - but no master in the stencil draws a version 2 shelf, so its module positions would be arithmetic rather than measurement. The numbering above is version 1's M0 to M2. This is a narrowing of what an earlier revision of this file claimed: it carried four evenly divided v2 openings, whose positions were computed rather than measured","rear":"drawing, as FRACTIONS only - the rear master is drawn sitting IN A RACK, with cabinet posts either side, so its bounding box is not the chassis and it fails gate 1 as an absolute source. This face carried a second decor, 444.5 x 8.0 at [0, 0] in #b4b6b8 - a full-width strip at the REAR of the top plate, with no counterpart on the bottom and no region naming it. asr9k-chassis drew it in this chassis's first commit, before the file split, and when asked could no longer say what sourced it; the best reconstruction was that it was meant as the rear lip of the top plate. APPLYING THE TEAM LEAD'S DISCRIMINATOR - does removing this make the drawing less true? - it fails. The rack mounting surface survives that test because a real plane is dimensioned in Figure 9 and necessarily cuts this face. An unsourced strip does not: nothing is lost by removing a mark that no document supports and no label describes, and something IS lost by keeping it, because a reader cannot tell it apart from the six-hundred other marks in this library that ARE sourced. THAT IS THE ACTUAL COST OF AN UNLABELLED FEATURE and it is why the same question about the ASR 9001's flanges was worth asking: an unlabelled mark is not just undocumented, it dilutes the ones that are. If the top plate does have a rear lip - and it plausibly does, since the exhaust is at the upper rear - it can be redrawn the moment a figure or a photograph shows it, with a region naming it. Deleting an unsourced mark is cheap and reversible; carrying it is neither.","rotate":"datasheet - this chassis mounts its cards HORIZONTALLY (see card-orientation), so each bay carries `rotate: 90` and the rotated footprint. No document we hold fixes which end of an ASR 9006 slot the ejector sits at - the guide says only \"ejector levers and captive screws at the left and right ends of each card\", i.e. BOTH ends - so 90 is the placeholder and the question is real. Its contract measures the PLATE at 42.05 x 362.24 mm inside a 395.7 mm envelope that is Cisco's stated line-card width \"including ejector bracket/lever\". Against this chassis: the plate's 362.24 mm covers the 352.59 mm cage opening with about 4.8 mm of overlap onto the rails each side, and its 42.05 mm sits inside the 46.61 mm slot pitch with about 4.5 mm of card guide. Both are what a filler plate should do, so the two measurements - taken independently, from different masters, by different people - corroborate rather than merely fail to contradict. Six slots of equal height divide that into a 46.605 mm pitch, which the guide's own figures support: Figure 3 and Figure 19 both draw all six rows the same height, because on this generation an RSP and a line card are the same form factor. A 9006 card is therefore 352.59 x 46.61 mm (13.88 x 1.835 in). Master \"ASR-9006-AC Front\" records width_in 1.9 and height_in 1.7500, i.e. 19.0 in over the flanges and 17.50 in tall. The four bays here follow the guide; the shelf's outer rectangle follows the stencil. Anyone re-measuring should expect that mismatch rather than treat it as an error","top-bottom-orientation":"SETTLED FROM THE FIGURE, and it is a convention rather than an error. Figure 9 (ASR 9006) and Figure 10 (ASR 9904) are both laid out with \"Rear of chassis\" printed at the TOP and \"Front of chassis\" at the BOTTOM, and the top and bottom views follow that layout. SO ON A TOP OR BOTTOM VIEW, y = 0 IS THE REAR AND y = depth IS THE FRONT. The rack-mounting-surface strip is therefore measured from y = depth, and the labels' \"from the front\" is correct as written. Stated here because the arithmetic reads as a 439.9 mm error to anyone who assumes y = 0 is the front, and it was read that way once already. The bottom view keeps the same depth axis as the top rather than mirroring it: looking at a chassis from below flips LEFT and RIGHT, not front and back, so a strip that runs the full width is unaffected either way - but anything left-right asymmetric on a bottom face would need the flip and does not have it yet, because nothing left-right asymmetric is drawn there. SEPARATELY FIXED: the strip is now CENTRED on the mounting plane. It used to be placed so that on the 9006 the dimension landed on its far edge and on the 9904 on its near edge - a 3.9 mm inconsistency in which edge of a 3.9 mm strip carried the number. CONVENTION, stated so it can be corrected in one line: this view is laid out as Figure 9 lays it out, front at the BOTTOM edge (y = 734.8) and rear at the top (y = 0), so the mounting surface line sits at 734.8 - 145.5 - 1.95 = 587.35, the strip being CENTRED on the plane rather than edged against it. Cisco's \"six power modules\" here is odd and is transcribed as printed rather than corrected. This chassis takes THREE on the version 1 power tray, which is what this manifest draws, or four on version 2 - never six. Either the datasheet is wrong or that row belongs to a larger chassis: the ASR 9010 has six bays and its own Table 13 row carries the identical wording. Treat 104.33 kg as a fully-configured figure of uncertain scope rather than one that can be reconciled against this chassis power system.
